DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review of "Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026" (The Copper Kettle)

The price increases are reasonable and mostly well supported. The menu-mix proposal rests on a factual error, and the projected figures overstate the gain.

**What checks out:**
- Every margin in Table 1 is correct as calculated.
- The £810 a week figure is correct: 310 × £1 + 260 × £1 + 120 × £2. Over 52 weeks that is £42,120.
- Each new price is below the midpoint of its competitor range (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50).
- The increases are modest: 6.1% on fish and chips, 6.7% on the burger and 7.7% on the steak.
- The steak rise is the best justified of the three. Steak has the weakest margin on the menu (60%), and beef is about to rise 12%.

## 1. The risotto has the *strongest* margin on the menu, not the weakest

Table 1 gives the risotto an **80%** margin, the highest of any dish. In cash terms it earns £11.20 a plate. That is more than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90), and close to fish and chips (£11.40).

Its sales of 90 plates a week tie with "other mains (specials)". But that line combines several dishes, so each special sells fewer than 90. The risotto is not the lowest seller per dish either.

The proposal would also *cost* money. The replacement special is priced the same as the risotto. If it earns the specials' current 64% margin, it makes £8.96 a plate, £2.24 less than the risotto. Across 90 plates that is about **£200 a week, or roughly £10,500 a year**, lost.

The dish that matches the description "weakest margin on the menu" is the steak, which the paper already addresses.

**Recommendation:** drop proposal 5.2, or rewrite it on a correct basis. If there is another reason to rotate the risotto, such as menu freshness, the replacement should be costed to earn at least £11.20 a plate.

## 2. VAT: the gross profit figures include it

The menu prices are consumer prices, so they include 20% VAT. A business serving about 1,050 mains a week is well above the VAT threshold.

Of each £1 price increase, about 83p reaches the restaurant. The projection should therefore read about **£675 a week, or £35,100 a year**, not £42,120. Restaurant gross profit is normally measured on prices net of VAT.

The same point applies to every margin in Table 1. On a net-of-VAT basis, fish and chips earns about 63%, not 69%. If the 70% target is also defined on VAT-inclusive prices, the comparisons with it are internally consistent, but the paper should say which basis it uses.

## 3. The 71% margin projection leaves out the beef rise and the risotto swap

Section 4 reports a 12% beef rise from 1 April, but none of the calculations use it.

**The £810 figure itself is unaffected.** It is the gain from raising prices compared with not raising them, and the beef rise hits both cases equally.

**The 71% margin figure is affected.** It describes the margin the restaurant will actually achieve, so the beef rise belongs in it. It also omits the risotto swap. Rough figures, on the paper's own VAT-inclusive basis:

| Scenario | Main-course margin |
|---|---|
| Today | about 69.4% |
| Price rises only (the paper's figure) | about 70.8% |
| Plus beef +12% | about 69.6% |
| Plus risotto replaced by a 64% special | about **68.5%** |

To produce these figures I assumed the specials sell for about £16 and that half the burger's food cost is beef. The result barely changes if those assumptions vary.

Taken as a whole, the package leaves main-course margin roughly where it is and below the 70% target, not at 71%.

## 4. "We remain the value option" is no longer true dish by dish

All three new prices fall below the competitors' midpoint. But each is now above the cheapest competitor:

| Dish | New price | Cheapest competitor |
|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £17.50 | £16.95 |
| Burger | £16.00 | £15.50 |
| Steak | £28.00 | £27.00 |

Today the Copper Kettle is the cheapest in the group on all three dishes. After the change it will be mid-priced. That may be the right position, but the paper should say so rather than imply nothing changes.

Also, the "midpoint" here is the midpoint of the price range, not the median of the five competitors, so it depends heavily on the single most expensive restaurant.

## 5. The volume assumption is asserted, not evidenced

- **Repeat bookings.** That 60% of bookings come from repeat guests shows a regular customer base. It doesn't show those guests will pay more, and regulars are the guests most likely to notice a price change. "Bookings" also excludes walk-ins, which are probably a larger share at lunch.
- **The 2024 price change.** "No visible effect on bookings" is offered without any figures, and the size of that increase isn't stated.
- **Lunch trade.** The paper calls weekday lunch "a small share of main-course sales" but gives no figure.
- **Break-even.** The useful number is how far volume can fall before the price rise loses money. Holding the beef rise constant, the break-even falls are roughly:
  - fish and chips: about 8%
  - burger: about 9%
  - steak: about 12%

  These are moderate thresholds. Some guests will also switch to the curry or risotto rather than leave, which softens any loss. Stating the break-even figures would let the owners judge the risk themselves.

## 6. The monitoring plan won't detect what it is meant to

- **Seasonality.** January and February are a quiet season. Spring trade, including Easter, will normally be higher, so a seasonal rise could hide a real fall in volume. Comparing against April and May 2025 would be better.
- **What is measured.** Plates per dish captures switching between dishes, not guests lost. Covers and bookings, especially from repeat guests, should be tracked too.
- **Decision rule.** There is none. State in advance what fall, sustained over what period, would lead to a rethink. The break-even figures in §5 are a natural threshold.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. Section 8 says "six trading days a week". The annual figure also assumes 52 trading weeks; check for closures.
- **Scope.** The 70% to 67% decline is across all courses, but the paper deals only with mains. It should say whether starters and desserts will be reviewed separately.
- **Data coverage.** The till data covers "every main course" only partly, because the specials are reported as one line.
- **Fish costs.** Fish and chips is the largest seller and fish prices are described as volatile. The paper notes this, but a sentence on what happens if fish costs rise would round out the risk section.
- **Not highlighting the increases.** This is reasonable commercially, and nothing more needs saying about it.

## What I'd change before it goes to the owners

1. Approve the three price increases. They are justified by rising costs and modest in size, and the competitor check is sound.
2. Drop or rewrite the risotto proposal, which is based on an error.
3. Restate the gain net of VAT (about £35,000 a year) and the margin after the beef rise (about 69.5%, not 71%).
4. Replace "we remain the value option" with an accurate statement of the new competitive position.
5. Add break-even volumes, a seasonally matched baseline, and a decision rule to the monitoring plan.
6. Fix the five-day versus six-day inconsistency.

The core recommendation, to raise these three prices, survives the review. The claims that the package is "well evidenced" and restores margin to about 71% do not.
